nameStory: The Tinder Polypore gets its name from its historical use as fire-starting material - the inner flesh was traditionally processed into a soft, fibrous tinder that could catch sparks from flint and steel. Indigenous peoples and early settlers prized this fungus as an essential survival tool, carrying pieces in their fire-making kits.
description: The Tinder Polypore is a hard, woody bracket fungus that grows like a shelf from the sides of dead and dying trees. These chunky, hoof-shaped brackets can range from fist-sized to dinner plate-sized, with a crusty gray-brown upper surface that looks almost charcoal-like. The fungus is rock-hard when fresh and becomes even harder with age, feeling almost like touching a piece of weathered wood or stone.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Hard, hoof-shaped bracket with a crusty, charcoal-gray to blackish upper surface that feels rough like tree bark. The top often has concentric ridges and may be cracked or furrowed with age.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Undersurface has tiny round pores (not gills) that are cream to pale brown when fresh, darkening with age. The pore surface feels smooth but firm to the touch.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Extremely hard and woody throughout - you could practically use it as a hammer. The flesh inside is rust-brown to cinnamon colored and fibrous when broken open.

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Grows directly from tree trunks without a stem, firmly attached like a shelf or bracket. Often found in overlapping clusters on the same tree.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a faint mushroomy smell, while older ones may smell slightly sweet or have no odor at all.

habitat: Look for Tinder Polypore on dead and dying hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, especially on birch, beech, and maple. It's commonly found along hiking trails, in mixed deciduous forests, and woodland edges from sea level to mountain elevations. The fungus can persist on the same dead tree for many years, often appearing alongside other bracket fungi.

seasonality.spring: Existing brackets from previous years are easily spotted as new growth begins. Fresh pore surfaces may appear creamy white on new growth.
seasonality.summer: Active growing season when new brackets form and expand. This is the best time to see the contrast between old charcoal-gray caps and newer, lighter-colored growth.
seasonality.fall: Peak visibility as leaves drop and brackets become more obvious on bare trees. New brackets harden and develop their characteristic dark crust.
seasonality.winter: Old brackets remain visible and identifiable on trees, though they're at their hardest. Snow may accumulate on the shelf-like caps, making them easier to spot from a distance.

funFact: This fungus was found in the gear of Ötzi the Iceman, the 5,300-year-old mummy discovered in the Alps, proving that humans have been using it as tinder for over five millennia - making it one of humanity's oldest documented survival tools!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Hoof Fungus (Fomes fomentarius), but Tinder Polypore has a darker, more charcoal-like upper surface and tends to be harder overall. Remember: if it looks like charcoal on top and feels like a rock, it's likely Tinder Polypore.
contextualKnowledge: **Note: I have limited confidence in some details about Fomes excavatus specifically, as this species may have taxonomic uncertainties or regional naming variations. Always cross-reference with local field guides and mycological societies for definitive identification.**
compareHints: Compared to its close relative Hoof Fungus, Tinder Polypore has a much darker, more blackened upper surface and tends to be significantly harder to the touch. Unlike Sweet Knot, which has a smoother, more rounded appearance, Tinder Polypore shows more pronounced ridging and cracking on its upper surface. All three species are extremely hard bracket fungi, but Tinder Polypore's charcoal-like coloring makes it the darkest of the group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relative the Tinder Polypore (Fomes excavatus), Hoof Fungus has a more pronounced bulbous shape rather than a flatter bracket form.
